speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We are in a much stronger fiscal position today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: However, building a new line remains a major decision due to the large upfront capital outlay involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This escalation in costs over time is not just due to inflation, but also because we are now building under more challenging conditions, for example, deeper MRT tunnels and stations amidst our increasingly built-up environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Although the development costs are hefty, the benefits extend over many generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The RIF will enable the Government to save up when our fiscal position allows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will smoothen out the large capital outlay for rail projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As the developer of the rail network in Singapore, LTA is well-placed to hold, manage and administer the RIF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clauses 4 and 6 of the Bill establish the RIF as a Statutory Fund under LTA and assign the function of managing the RIF to LTA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 6 further sets out the sources of money for the RIF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This enables the Government to set aside money from the Consolidated Fund or Development Fund for the RIF through Supply Law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 6 also defines the purposes for which LTA is empowered to withdraw moneys from the RIF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Essentially, this ensures that the RIF is only used for the development of the MRT and Light Rail Transit (LRT) network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The key uses of the RIF are as follows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: First, to expand the MRT and LRT network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This includes constructing rail infrastructure, such as stations, tunnels and tracks; acquiring the first set of operating assets, such as trains; performing investigative studies; as well as associated costs, such as the cost of land.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The RIF may also be used to replace existing operating assets, if such replacement is required to operate the expanded rail network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: For example, when we build rail extensions that connect to existing lines, operating assets on the existing lines may need to be replaced to allow both sections to interface properly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Second, to replace, upgrade and add rail infrastructure, such as tunnels and tracks, for existing rail lines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The development of a rail line does not end after it is constructed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will need to continually invest in the upgrading and renewal of the rail civil infrastructure as they age, to ensure safe and reliable operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: These renewal works will similarly require large capital outlays.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It is prudent for us to put aside money in anticipation of such spending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Third, to invest in accordance with the standard power of investment for Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is to enable the RIF to keep up with inflation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The investments made using the RIF moneys will be held within the RIF, to ensure that the proceeds continue to be ringfenced for the development of the MRT and LRT network.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, the moneys in the Railway Sinking Fund (RSF), which is another Statutory Fund under LTA, may also be used to acquire operating assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 5 distinguishes the use of the RIF from the RSF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The RIF is intended for the expansion of the rail network and the acquisition of the first set of operating assets necessary to enable this expansion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: On the other hand, the RSF is intended for the renewal of rail operating assets, such as trains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This distinction reflects the allocation of financial responsibility between taxpayers and commuters – tax dollars will be used to invest in the civil infrastructure and the first set of operating assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Thereafter, every generation of commuters will need to pay part of the recurrent cost of operating the rail network, including the renewal of operating assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This ensures that the burden on taxpayers remains sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This represents a sizeable proportion of daily commute on our public transportation system, and these numbers are expected to rise in the near future when our total rail capacity is further expanded with the opening of new train lines.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The NRFF is meant to create a more reliable system where maintenance regimes of train operators are regulated by the enhanced Maintenance Performance Standards.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In principle, the NRFF should have a positive impact on rail reliability since it increases the onus of preventative maintenance on the network operators.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These incidents do not seem to gel with the pledge that the Singapore MRT (SMRT) and LTA made in July 2016 that they would increase the headcount of maintenance and engineering staff to meet the enhanced standards.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I hope that MOT could give the House perhaps an update on whether SMRT and LTA are on track to increase their maintenance capacity, how the Ministry is holding SMRT and LTA responsible for adhering to the Maintenance Performance Standards, and perhaps the consequences they face for not doing so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In principle, RIF is meant to allow the Government to save when the fiscal position allows, so as to finance the development of new rail lines and to renew and upgrade existing rail infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Minister can provide clarification on the financing model of the RIF to meet future needs beyond the initial capital injection of $5 billion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to inquire if the Ministry has developed a set of financing guidelines for the fund and whether it will be making these guidelines known.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The topic of public transport, Sir, is not just a critical one, but it also somewhat an emotive one because it affects everyone in one way or another.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore continues to upgrade and enhance our rail and network system, we need to build in a rubric of checks and balances to ensure that our investments are reaping due returns in the form of enhanced performance and reliability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has the Government then predetermined a set of expenditure-performance ratios to measure the returns of capital expenditure from the RIF vis-à-vis the expected improvement in train reliability and performance?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Aside from setting up the expenditure-performance ratio, has a set of asset replacement guidelines been drawn up to ensure that capital equipment is replaced or bought before the need to do so becomes pressing?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, lifts in public housing estates are generally replaced when they hit the 28-year mark or thereabouts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the lifespan of rail assets before they are being replaced and how is the operational lifespan of these assets determined?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are setting aside the RIF to fund current expenditure, I think it is also good that the RIF will form one of the foundational pillars to ensure that we have a reliable public transport system to meet future capacity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Sir, I end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The costs for rail infrastructure development have risen sharply over the years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Inflation aside, the real costs for rail development will continue to rise because our rail development now takes place in a highly built-up environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And as our rail network grows, we will always be renewing some part of the system which will also be costly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, in this light, the RIF is a timely move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We want to avoid raising taxes substantially or borrowing at perhaps unfavourable rates when the time comes to make these investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Provided that the Government can commit to prudently setting aside this money, the RIF will help us to finance these important infrastructure developments at the lowest possible cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is a move that makes our transport finances future-ready.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are also other challenges involved in ensuring that our transport system is future-ready.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is nearly double that of the present network.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The RIF will provide us the financial capability to pay for these important investments, but we must also have the human resource capability to operate and maintain the systems and we must have the public support that commuters and taxpayers alike are willing to pay for the upkeep of the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This followed a 2012 review by SMRT that identified a need to triple the engineering strength to handle the maintenance, renewal and operations of future MRT lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, tripling your engineering staff strength in just a few years means that the majority of our rail engineers today are relative newcomers in the field.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But experience and expertise do take time to develop, and the question is why was the engineering strength in our core public transport operators allowed to remain at levels that are manifestly inadequate to the task?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Under the old financing model for public transport, operators had to survive based on profits from the very narrow margin between fare revenue and operating costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Since there is little that our operators can do to raise the fare revenue side of the box, they had to keep costs down.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Maintenance and operations are cost centres, so the pressure naturally fell on engineering to do more and more with less and less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The old public transport financing model was designed to push operators to minimise costs and, hence, to minimise the fare burden on the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And because of that, we paid relatively little to operate a world-class transport system while the system was new.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we ended up paying for it later through deferred maintenance and poor reliability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And, today, our rail operators are also paying the price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is not hard to see the danger in this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has already done so with the Bus Contracting Model for our bus operators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is not about rescuing shareholders or private companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is about ensuring that our rail operators and their core engineering capabilities have the resources needed to thrive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, we must ensure there are incentives to remain efficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A young talented Singaporean must see rail engineering as a viable long-term career where they can make a real difference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: With support from the right Government financial and training framework, our public transport operators can build the human resource capabilities for our future rail system needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, let me touch on the issue of public support for these investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Planning for our original MRT system took place in the public eye.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The final decision to proceed with a rail-based system was only made in 1982.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The high costs of a rail-based system, versus an all-bus system, were the sticking point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think we are all glad that the Government made the decision to invest in the MRT.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the point is that the public was aware of, and publicly debated, these decisions to spend billions of dollars on rail infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I am concerned that we lack a similar level of public engagement and shared responsibility for decision-making in the transport system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Senior Minister of State for Transport is now chairing the Land Transport Master Plan 2040 public consultation exercise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I would suggest that we go beyond current efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue to involve the public as a co-creator of decisions made in public transport, ranging from investing in MRT lines, to determining the quality of service offered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These decisions have cost implications and the public is ultimately paying the bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This question of public support for our transport system has often been framed as one of commuter satisfaction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I think that is a narrow definition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If you put huge subsidies into the system and you greatly improve quality, as the Government has done in recent years, then, of course, the commuter will be satisfied, or at least more satisfied.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the problem is that today, the commuter may be satisfied without having any idea of the real costs and tradeoffs involved in providing a world-class transport system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Commuters may not realise that their fares are low, because they are only asked to pay today for a relatively small part of the operating costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think the Government must set out a clear long-term vision of how commuters will contribute to the longer-term funding and investment decisions for public transport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It means that when the public enjoys better connectivity and less crowded rides, they share in the costs of providing these services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But now that the public pays part of these system costs, they must also have a way to say when they have had enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want to force people to buy business class tickets when what they really want is economy – or premium economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are no market forces that would allow commuters to tell us what is the right mix of quality and price in public transport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government can assure us that, in addition to financial capacity building, equally strong measures will be taken to build human resource capabilities and public engagement and support for our public transport system.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Before I start, on behalf of my residents who use the North-South (N-S) Line, I would like to thank MOT, our MRT workers, as well as those involved with the N-S Line upgrade for their countless hours of hard work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, can LTA share how we determine on the lifespan of the key assets and system?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we draw on the lessons over the last decade or so, the key issue is how do we ensure timely upgrades, as well as preventive maintenance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Does LTA determine this lifespan through international benchmarks or through LTA's internal assessment working with engineering consultancy companies?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If LTA relies on international benchmarks, can LTA share which country and which system did we use?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And when we localise those benchmarks for use locally, do we account for Singapore-specific conditions, such as our heat and humidity levels?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, I strongly agree with the previous Member's view that our people will need to understand, not just the quality of service, but how much it costs them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in our medical bills, we reflect the true cost, and then we reflect the subsidies, before arriving at the amount that Singaporeans have to pay.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That is a good approach to keeping Singaporeans informed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This cost should include components, such as infrastructure investment cost as well as total operating cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is important information for our citizens and, I suspect, will shape our discussions in our Chamber over time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we cannot just talk about satisfaction levels, but also whether or not, like the previous Member said, are we overconsuming or under-consuming transportation resources.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I assume that the Sinking Fund is for existing lines and the Infrastructure Fund is for new lines.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Demolition and replacement expenses of any rail line is likely to be a major expenditure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When will LTA charge these under the Sinking Fund and when will it do so under the Infrastructure Fund?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding my few queries, I support the amendment Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our land transport system is becoming more complex, and commuters have increasingly diverse travel needs and preferences.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to make difficult tradeoffs in deciding how to plan and develop our land transport network.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Walter Theseira that the Government needs to engage the public when planning and developing our land transport system to develop public support and to ensure the land transport system continues to be designed with commuters in mind.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is why we have embarked on an extensive public consultation exercise, as part of developing the Land Transport Master Plan (LTMP) for 2040.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Over the last two months, many Singaporeans have shared their concerns and aspirations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some have participated in our Focus Group Discussions and LTA is gaining valuable feedback through this process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA is also taking the opportunity to share its planning considerations and tradeoffs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Please continue to come forward and participate through the LTMP consultation process so that, together, through partnership, we do achieve the best possible outcomes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Henry Kwek suggested that LTA communicate the true cost of providing MRT services so that citizens understand the financial tradeoffs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are not able to issue receipts for each ride, so we use other ways to communicate the cost and subsidies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to communicate to commuters the cost of providing public transport services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Darryl David asked about the differences between the RIF and RSF.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Instead, the RSF is to be used to acquire operating assets, such as trains and signalling systems, to replace or upgrade ageing ones for existing rail lines.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the other hand, the RIF is, by this Bill, to be used to expand and renew our domestic rail infrastructure, such as tracks and tunnels.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Beyond the injection of $5 billion in FY2018, the RIF can be topped up in future years when the fiscal position allows.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA integrates our transport plan closely with the land use plan and builds new rail lines only when there is a strong use case.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This good planning and financial principle does not change with the introduction of RIF.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The RIF simply provides the Government with the flexibility to save up, when our fiscal position allows, in anticipation of lumpy capital rail investments in future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Darryl David also asked how LTA determines when to replace and upgrade key assets and systems in a timely manner.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA determines the replacement schedule of our rail assets based on the asset design life and the specific asset’s actual condition.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is to take into account variance in lifespan under Singapore’s operating environment, as Mr Kwek correctly noted.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where necessary, LTA also engages engineering experts to provide third-party opinions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Going forward, LTA is developing the Rail Enterprise Asset Management System, which will integrate asset information and maintenance records across the different systems, so that the health of the various operating assets can be monitored holistically over their respective lifecycles.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The system will be equipped with data analytics capabilities to monitor asset performance and identify potential faults before they occur, so that these assets can be repaired or renewed pre-emptively.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This shift towards data-driven predictive maintenance and asset renewal will enable sustained rail reliability, while optimising overall lifecycle costs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Darryl David asked whether SMRT and LTA have sufficient maintenance capacity to achieve high rail reliability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira made some remarks and asked some questions about human capital development.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I want to assure this House that MOT, LTA and our rail operators are working hard to raise rail reliability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: SMRT has already raised its maintenance headcount by more than 700, as has been noted by Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, since its transition to the New Rail Financing Framework.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Theseira also correctly noted that it takes time to train and groom our engineers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are also partnering our institutes of higher learning and centralised academies, such as the Singapore Rail Academy, to roll out workforce development programmes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But maintenance capability is not only about manpower.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is also about giving our engineers and technicians sufficient engineering hours to carry out these maintenance and asset renewal works.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is why we introduced Early Closures and Late Openings (ECLO) last December.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The commuters have felt the improvement and I thank Mr Henry Kwek for his comments.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: His residents have given him good feedback about the reliability of the N-S Line.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As the new signalling system for the East-West (E-W) Line stabilises, residents living in the East and West will also begin to enjoy better rail reliability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a bold target and very few metro systems around the world have consistently achieved this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOT, LTA and our operators will continue to work hard to bring commuters safe, reliable and affordable public transport services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Theseira observed that we need a framework that allows our rail operators to be financially sustainable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is so that they can continue to attract engineers to join the industry and to invest to sustain high rail reliability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Under this model, the Government co-shares the fare revenue risk with the operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a big step towards building financial sustainability that Assoc Prof Theseira spoke about.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will need to evolve our financing model to continue to adapt to the changing operating environment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Government will continue to review our financing framework periodically to ensure the public transport system continues to serve us well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It would be one of the most expensive infrastructure projects for our young nation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It was a difficult decision but the right one.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When these lines started operations in 1987, they opened up new possibilities for Singaporeans to live, work and play.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have since expanded the rail network considerably.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The improved connectivity brought about by our rail network has allowed us to develop new economic centres and key facilities across our island.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The implementation and success of Punggol Digital District, Changi Business Park, Changi Airport, Tuas industrial estate and Jurong Lake District, would not be possible without the enhanced connectivity brought about by the rail network.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The rail system is an economic project and a social leveller.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As Mr Darryl David pointed out, Singaporeans depend on the MRT and LRT – 3.5 million trips are made on the rail network every day, bringing Singaporeans to school, work and back home.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, this rail network has grown to become the backbone of our public transport system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because of the foresight of the previous generation, our economic opportunities have expanded and our island home is now more connected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In setting up the RIF, we are following in their footsteps and planning for the future of the next generation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.06 pm until 3.30 pm.
